newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe shares continue climb despite strike.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe shares continue climb despite strike.

text.p: Zimbabwe's share market continued shrugging off an unprecedented crippling strike by civil servants with brokers saying on Wednesday the good news outweighed the bad to maintain the stocks' march ahead.
The key 57-share industrial index -- which has been scaling historic heights since last Friday -- rose 12.15 points to close at 5,718.16, a new all time peak.

"I think the good news outweighs the bad. We had some very good news on interest rates coming down and that's what people, especially locals, are more interested in," said Anthony Barfoot, Zimbabwe Stock Exchange (ZSE) chief executive.

Hopes that high borrowing rates of around 30 percent were coming down were raised last week when the central Reserve Bank lowered its key rediscount rate to 27.5 percent from 29.5 percent, citing falling annual inflation, pegged at 22 percent in July.
Barfoot said the civil servants strike -- which has paralysed essential social services -- might have had a greater impact if it had spread to the private industry.

"Foreign fund managers have been trading as usual... It's business as usual until the market knows whether the serious stance the government has taken against the strikers will be effected, whether it will lay off hundreds of workers or compromise," one broker said.

The government said at the weekend it had dismissed the strikers -- estimated by the Public Service Association at 70 to 80 percent of the country's 180,000-strong civil service -- for defying an order to go back to work.
Another broker said the lack of an impact on trade on the ZSE might be due to a scarcity of news on the strike -- apart from government statements -- in the state-controlled media.
"The local media has tended to gloss over it so people don't have much detail of what's going on. Maybe the weekly papers will have more," she said.

On the ZSE on Wednesday, multi-industrial group IHL jumped 200 cents to 3,400, bankers FMB rose 50 cents to 2,800 while five-cent gains were registered by hotel chain Zimsun at 340, clothing retailer Truworths at 615, paper mill KCI at 40, engineering firm Gulliver at 115, pork processor Colcom at 255, tyre manufacturer Dunlop at 160 and textiler David Whitehead at 55.
But tobacco company BAT bucked the trend, dropping 50 cents to 1,050 and building firm J and F lost 20 cents to 150.
Minings were also firmer with nickel giant Bindura gaining 50 cents to 1,075 while Wankie Colliery and Falgold put on five cents each to 310 and 170.
The seven-share mining index added 5.57 points to 1,277.01.
